Hi Team,

We have customer and they were hit by an outage last week because of an issue with one of our DC. They want to primarily find out a way to exclude the impacted DC by modifying the PAC file.

Following are the details of their environment:

3000 users
 250 locations; No static IPs(can’t use ${SRCIP}); distributed across North America
 Zapp is deployed in tunnel with Local Proxy mode

I have written the following code which will go into their App Profile PAC file to get the job done. I want your help in locating any caveats with the following code:

//Find the primary node IP address
 var withPort = “${GATEWAY}?;

//${GATEWAY} resolves to 165.225.106.36:80 so to replace the port I am using substring function

var gatewayIp = withPort.substring(0, 14);

//send traffic to secondary gateway if primary node is the impacted one

if (shExpMatch(gatewayIp, “165.225.106.36?)) return “PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:443; DIRECT?;

//If the primary Gateway is not the affected gateway traffic will flow the nearest DC

return “PROXY ${GATEWAY}:443; PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:443; DIRECT?;

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn3ICAQ/user-auth-is-not-happening-for-specific-client-ips","lastmod":"2023-05-31T08:53:47.000Z","id":"0D54u00009evn3ICAQ"} -->
## User auth is not happening for specific client IP's

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn3ICAQ/user-auth-is-not-happening-for-specific-client-ips
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2018-11-23T08:21:18.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-05-31T08:53:47.000Z
- Answers: 1
- Likes: 0
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

Hi,

Recently we observed for one client IP 10.205.216.135 user auth is not working. But from the same segment for other IP’s(for ex:10.205.216.134) user auth is working fine.

On digging further we got to know the TCP 3way handshake is not happening for auth URL [gateway.zscalertwo.net](http://gateway.zscalertwo.net) and user is getting timeout.

We captured the packet for the user IP 10.205.216.135 and [gateway.zscalertwo.net](http://gateway.zscalertwo.net) IP 199.168.151.10 on firewall and observed the TCP SYN packet is passing firewall and going to GRE tunnel but response is not coming from GRE tunnel.

As a workaround we have changed user IP to 10.205.216.137, post that I can see user auth worked successfully and everything worked as expected.

Is anyone facing similar issue. If yes, please let me know the root cause and how it is resolved.
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

## Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) and Application Layer Gateway (ALG) enabled applications

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn4aCAA/zscaler-internet-access-zia-and-application-layer-gateway-alg-enabled-applications
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2018-07-24T10:25:51.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-05-31T08:54:00.000Z
- Answers: 8
- Likes: 0
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

The best practice for customers using IPSEC/GRE tunnels is to send all ports and protocols through the tunnels. However, there are some protocols that currently cannot be properly handled by the Zscaler nodes. These protocols require an “Application Layer Gateway? feature in order to be properly handled by a firewall.

**What is the Application Layer Gateway feature?**

Some protocols use separate data and communication channels for the transmission. The communication channel can contain information about ephemeral TCP/UDP ports used by the data channel and information about client/server IP address. In general, the Application Layer Gateway (ALG) allows the network device to check the application payload in order to convert the network layer address information, synchronize between multiple streams/sessions of data between two hosts exchanging data or recognize application-specific commands and offer granular security controls over them. The ALG feature can be used for multiple protocols like MSRPC, SUNRPC, SQL, SIP, RTSP, H323, MGCP, SCCP, FTP etc.
 Here is an example of how the ALG feature handles SIP/H323 protocol:
 *SIP/H323 protocol requires special handling when passing through a Stateful Packet Inspection (SPI) firewall. Firewalls need ALG to handle SIP/H323 protocols. When the phone starts the call, it makes a connection to the PBX server on UDP port 5060. This is used as the control connection to exchange the audio connection ports between the phone and PBX. The SPI firewall needs to intercept this connection and learn the audio exchange ports/IP addresses and open the inbound and outbound ports dynamically. This is handled by the ALG feature.*

More information about the ALG can be found in the articles below:

en.wikipedia.org
##### [Application-level gateway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Application-level_gateway)

An application-level gateway (ALG, also known as application layer gateway, application gateway, application proxy, or application-level proxy) is a security component that augments a firewall or NAT employed in a computer network. It allows customized NAT traversal filters to be plugged into the gateway to support address and port translation for certain application layer "control/data" protocols such as FTP, BitTorrent, SIP, RTSP, file transfer in IM applications. In order for these proto An AL...

[https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2694](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2694)

**How Zscaler handles the traffic which requires the ALG feature?**
 Currently, Zscaler Cloud Firewall supports the ALG feature for the following two protocols:
 -Passive FTP
 -PPTP

The ALG support for other protocols is in our road-map, but currently, protocols for which the ALG feature is not implemented on the Zscaler cloud firewall (like Active FTP, SIP or VOIP) should be bypassed from Zscaler.
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

## Google shows origin from India (or any other country) for us-based ZScaler customer

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn4hCAA/google-shows-origin-from-india-or-any-other-country-for-usbased-zscaler-customer
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2018-07-02T13:29:32.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-05-31T09:08:34.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 1
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

We have an issue with [google.com](http://google.com), [amazon.com](http://amazon.com) landing pages we get redirected to India even though we use ZScaler nodes in the US and our public ip’s are US-registered.

ZScaler support has suggested the following work around for the issue:

1. Enable SSL scanning on the location.
2. Enable SSL scanning on Google traffic only. If you are using PAC you can add the following exception in your PAC file.

if (dnsDomainIs(host, “[google.com](http://google.com)?))
 return “PROXY ${GATEWAY}:80; PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:80; DIRECT?;

1. You can bookmark “[http://www.google.co/ncr](http://www.google.co/ncr)?. By using this, you will not get re-directed to incorrect Google domain or any other page. This is a method which Google provides to over-ride the default re-directed page provided by Google to a page of your choice.
2. Create a new custom category and add "google.co.in " in it. Refer to Zscaler Admin UI > Administration > URL Categories. Now go to URL policy and block this new custom category and redirect it to [Google](http://www.google.com/ncr). Refer to Zscaler Admin UI > Policy > URL & Cloud App Control > URL Filtering Policy.

I was just wondering if any other customers experience a similar issue?

Is there a way to resolve this w/o the blocking policy?

Thanks,
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn50CAA/running-kerberos-with-a-vzen","lastmod":"2023-05-31T09:07:54.000Z","id":"0D54u00009evn50CAA"} -->
## Running Kerberos with a vZEN

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn50CAA/running-kerberos-with-a-vzen
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2018-05-14T11:14:34.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-05-31T09:07:54.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 1
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

Hi All,

Just thought I’d share some learnings from a recent POC deployment we’ve done for a customer when running Kerberos Auth with a vZEN. I know that the Product Manager for this area is getting the documentation updated, but just incase someone else runs across the same issue, I figured I would share our learnings.

1. You need to request that support enables Kerberos Authentication for vZENs in the backend via ZADMIN. The fastest way to find out if the appropriate setting is enabled is to run “sudo vzen troubleshoot netstat? from the command line, and check to see that the vZEN is listening on “*.8800?.

This is required so that:

- The vZEN will listen on port 8800
- So that the vZEN will enable SPNEGO auth (kerberos authentication)
- Zscaler publish the vZEN FQDN publicly in DNS (details @[Zscaler Help](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/deploying-kerberos-vzens))

1. Normal authentication bypasses won’t work when explicitly proxying to port 8800. These either need to be bypassed in Administration->Cloud Configuration-> Kerberos Authentication Exemption, or proxied on a standard port to the vZEN via a PAC file.
2. [IP.ZSCALER.COM](http://IP.ZSCALER.COM) won’t show up any authentication details for users accessing it with Kerberos. This is because it relies on Cookie based authentication to provide the login info. Also when using a vZEN, IP will tell you that you are going direct to the service, as the vZEN does not include an XFF header, to prevent leakage of your internal IPs. If in doubt, contact support, or use “sudo vzen troubleshoot netstat? from the CLI to verify that you’re seeing traffic connect.
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn53CAA/a-remote-webserver-has-blacklisted-my-favorite-zscaler-enforcement-node-what-can-i-do","lastmod":"2023-07-06T11:47:16.000Z","id":"0D54u00009evn53CAA"} -->
## A remote webserver has blacklisted my favorite Zscaler Enforcement Node. What can I do?

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn53CAA/a-remote-webserver-has-blacklisted-my-favorite-zscaler-enforcement-node-what-can-i-do
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2018-05-10T18:32:55.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-07-06T11:47:16.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 3
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

**Issue**: When a web server that is popular in a particular region receives a strong stream of traffic from a single IP address, such as that of a ZEN (Zscaler Enforcement Node), its webmaster may suspect a threat and blacklist the IP address, which in this case, is the egress IP address of the ZEN. So instead of serving content for requests originating from the ZEN, the web server might reset the connection or just not respond.

**Solution**: If this occurs, contact Zscaler Support. Zscaler will reach out to the site’s webmaster, explain the nature of our service, and request the removal of the ZEN IP address from the blacklist. Additionally, Zscaler highly recommends that you contact the web site as well and ask the webmaster to remove the ZEN IP address from their blacklist. We have found this approach to be highly effective.

To view the list of Zscaler public node IP addresses, go to ips..net and view the Cloud Enforcement Node Ranges page. To learn how you can find your cloud name, click [here](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/what-my-cloud-name).

When you contact the webmaster, give them the data center IP ranges in the Actual Usable Range column. It contains less IP addresses than the CIDR Notation column.

[[337795d2-e349-488b-aca9-be387a4ad9c0_display] 337795d2-e349-488b-aca9-be387a4ad9c0_display855×771 325 KB](https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/servlet/servlet.FileDownload?file=0154u000009O5NGAA0)

Note that the webmasters at the remote website will need time to respond and to remove the ZEN IP address from the blacklist. In the meantime, you can try the following options to restore connectivity to the website immediately.

Only in the rarest cases do we see a user’s secondary ZEN blacklisted in addition to their primary ZEN. If your organization uses PAC files, we recommend adding a rule in the PAC file that routes traffic to that particular website through the next-closest ZEN. One way to do this is with the dnsDomainIs() function shown below:

if (dnsDomainIs(host, “.remote-server.name?)) return “PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY}; DIRECT?;
 This allows traffic to that web server to continue going through the Zscaler service.

Alternatively, you can add a rule in the PAC file that forwards traffic directly to the web server, bypassing the Zscaler service. You can specify this with the dnsDomainIs() function as well, shown below:

if (dnsDomainIs(host, “.remote-server.name?)) return “DIRECT?;
 Additionally, you can also configure a Zscaler service bypass through the proxy configuration menu in most browsers.
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

---

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn5HCAQ/apple-caching-and-zscaler-internet-access","lastmod":"2023-05-31T09:07:51.000Z","id":"0D54u00009evn5HCAQ"} -->
## Apple Caching and Zscaler Internet Access

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evn5HCAQ/apple-caching-and-zscaler-internet-access
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2018-02-23T16:09:23.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-05-31T09:07:51.000Z
- Answers: 1
- Likes: 1
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

Apple devices (macOS X, & iOS) periodically retrieve updates from Apple and to reduce load on multi-user networks, Apple offers a caching service that can be run on Apple servers. This is Apple’s description of the service: [Change Content Caching settings on Mac - Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/about-content-caching-mchleaf1e61d/mac). In summary when an Apple device looks to the cloud for software it will first check in with Apple to see if there is a caching server on the local network that can be used. If there is a caching server then the Apple device in question will contact that caching server for software rather than reaching out to the cloud. The key in this decision is the source IP that the Apple device is using when it first contacts Apple.

When Zscaler Internet Access cloud is used to protect a multi-user network the source IP that devices use will be a Zscaler IP address rather than the true public source IP of the client network. Therefore, if Apple caching is a desired function within a network there is some configuration required to facilitate this service.

As of the date of this post two hostnames are used to detect the client source IP address, and they resolve to the respective IP addresses as shown below:
 **[lcdn-locator.apple.com](http://lcdn-locator.apple.com)**
 17.164.1.38
 17.164.1.41
 17.146.232.38
 17.146.232.42

**[serverstatus.apple.com](http://serverstatus.apple.com)**
 17.171.49.71
 17.171.49.180
 17.146.1.21
 17.146.1.147
 17.146.6.10

These IP addresses may change or differ around the world as you can see by using a tool like [www.whatsmydns.net](http://www.whatsmydns.net) or [dns.google.com](http://dns.google.com).

To enable Apple caching we need to ensure that requests from clients to these two hostnames will reach the Internet from the true client source IP. There are a few options:

- If explicitly forwarding traffic via PAC file as the only way to reach Zscaler these hostnames can be exempted within the PAC file. This strategy could also work in a Zscaler App deployment where a PAC file is used.
- If Zscaler Enforcement Nodes (ZENs) have been deployed on premise, PAC files can be used to direct these specific hostnames to the local PZEN or VZEN clusters so that sessions will be sourced from those local nodes.
- If sessions are forwarded transparently at a router or SD-WAN appliance the above IP addresses (or whatever the current IP addresses are) should be exempted from forwarding. If the specific IP addresses are entered into a configuration it is recommended that a script or other systematic method is implemented to monitor for change in the future.
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

In this case, the customer is using a custom app that uses Google maps to display their building locations etc. It seems that all of the data is pulled by [googleapis.com](http://googleapis.com) on http and not https. Traffic goes out of the PC via GRE to Zscaler. The app in use requires IP surrogacy to work. The IP is set to expire at 8 hours, then it breaks. It is not until they do some browsing via https that [ip.zscaler.com](http://ip.zscaler.com) shows them as logged in again and then the app starts working again. Enabling xff did not help. Currently, they are not doing TLS interception

Notes Regarding IP surrogacy:
 Requirements
 • To use this feature, your organization must use one of the following methods to forward traffic to the service:
 ○ A GRE or IPsec tunnel without NAT (met)
 ○ Forward proxy chaining with the XFF Forwarding option enabled on the location (enabled temporarily, did not cause surrogacy to kick in)
 ○ Your organization subscribes to a dedicated proxy port (cannot check as zadmin is down)
 • The location must have authentication enabled. (met)

So, what can we do to make this work without a user visiting a https site or something to kick off authentication and getting the surrogate IP assigned? These are kiosks and they are only ever browsed by the app and only goes to the limited sites built into that. They also mentioned the computers reboot everynight. Could we run an automated task or maybe a powershell script to get that IP going again?
 Thanks!

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evnDdCAI/when-allow-due-to-insufficient-app-data-log-entry-value-appears-and-when-it-does-not","lastmod":"2024-12-09T15:00:35.000Z","id":"0D54u00009evnDdCAI"} -->
## When "allow due to insufficient app data" log entry value appears and when it does not

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evnDdCAI/when-allow-due-to-insufficient-app-data-log-entry-value-appears-and-when-it-does-not
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2021-07-19T17:35:09.000Z
- Last activity: 2024-12-09T15:00:35.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 7
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

**The log entry will NOT appear if the DPI simply failed to detect the application**

The Admin will NOT see the “Allow due to insufficient app data" indication under the “Action" column in the logs if the DPI (network application) failed to detect after 12 packets.

If the network application wasn’t detected after 12 packets then the Advanced Cloud Firewall (ACFW) will try to match on the “leaf" data already assembled: so TCP + SSL/TLS + HTTPS for example when a complete leaf might look like TCP + SSL/TLS + HTTPS + Salesforce (with Salesforce as the network app in this example). If there was a rule for either TCP or SSL/TLS or HTTPS then that indication will be given in the logs instead.

**The conditions when the log entry appears:**

The Admin will only see the “Allow due to insufficient app data" indication under the “Action" column in the logs if the session was terminated gracefully or suddenly before the network application identification process could finish. The network application identification process occurs on or before the 12th packet but mostly between packets 2 to 5 and as counted from those sent from the user /session-initiator perspective.

Getting the “Allow due to insufficient app data" indication assumes the ACFW rule was ranked appropriately versus other possible ACFW rules so that TCP and then SSL/TLS and then HTTPS were not blocked prior to the rule with the Salesforce application identification failure. It is these few (more than 1 but less than 13) packets associated to the precursor identification “leaves" that was the *allowed* traffic referenced by “allow due to insufficient app data".

As distinct from network applications, network services are just protocol (TCP, UDP) + dest:port and so always match on the first packet. The user will never see an “Allow due to insufficient app data?? message because of a network service condition in a CFW rule.

[image]Network Application usage best practices

The use of network applications in Advanced CFW rules is a tradeoff between certainty (network applications are the highest confidence identifications) and delay (can identify as late as the 12th packet of any given flow or not at all).

When a rule has a network application, then all qualifying flows will potentially match the rule until the network application is identified and the condition is either true or false. It is therefore recommended that whenever possible:

1. If the network application is part of a higher ordered rule then blend the network application condition with at least one other condition that makes the rule “qualify" to a very limited number of sessions/flows. For example, add a destination IP address to the rule so the DPI engine only tries to identify network apps destined to that IP (as a logical “AND" condition). Add a user condition, add a network services condition, etc. The more conditions the more specific the DPI identification is applied;
2. If network applications are the only condition in the firewall rule then order the rule lower than rules where a first packet identifications are possible (in particular below rules where block actions occur since this traffic is never wanted). This allows for those higher ordered rules to match and take their configured action and only a subset of all flows remain for examination as part of the network application DPI identification.

Please see [Best Practice for CFW Rules with Network Application Detections as Conditions](https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000A0dGk2CQE/best-practice-for-cfw-rules-with-network-application-dpi-detections-as-condition) for more information
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

My specific use case at the moment is related to users accessing ChatGPT. I’ve set up a Cloud Application policy for ChatGPT to move users into a specific Browser Isolation policy, which I’ve set up with the following settings:

- Auto proxy config to the Zscaler Cloud proxy pac file
- using the Zscaler Root Certificate
- Blocks copy and paste to/from
- Blocks file transfer to/from
- Read-Only Isolation is disabled (also tested with enabled)
- View Office files in Isolation is disabled
- Local Browser Rendering is enabled
- All Isolation Regions enabled
- Browser-in-browser experience (also tested with native browser)
- Cookie Persistence enabled (also tested with cookie persistence disabled)

I check the box, and then it just moves into a cycle of the site checking the browser and then prompted for the captcha challenge. The ZIA logs aren’t showing that anything is being blocked at this point, so I’m a bit stumped. I figured the Local Rendering option was the culprit, but there has been no change between it being enabled or disabled. Is this going to be a situation where I have to set up a Cloud App rule to specifically allow Cloudflare under the DNS over HTTPS category? Anyone else have ideas for this?

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009eykQLCAY/bing-chatgpt-feature-is-not-working-through-zscaler","lastmod":"2023-06-05T04:51:35.000Z","id":"0D54u00009eykQLCAY"} -->
## Bing ChatGPT feature is not working through Zscaler

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009eykQLCAY/bing-chatgpt-feature-is-not-working-through-zscaler
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-03-29T15:45:41.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-06-05T04:51:35.000Z
- Answers: 2
- Likes: 1
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

Bing has recently rolled out a new AI feature with ChatGPT. This feature is accessible when using the “Bing Discover” plug-in that comes with Microsoft Edge. When using ZIA with full SSL inspection, you can expect the “Bing Discover” plug-in to display an error message.

[[image] image441×848 13.5 KB](https://global.discourse-cdn.com/zscaler/original/2X/7/780683c01528bc695d2d7494329d1d87b31b43a6.png)

To resolve this issue, follow the steps below:

1. Open your ZIA admin portal and navigate to Policy > SSL Inspection [11]
2. Click “Add an SSL Inspection Rule”. Click the drop down on “URL Categories” and click the + icon to add a new URL Category. NOTE: Ensure this rule is above any “SSL inspect all traffic” rules. [[22] 22773×705 34.3 KB](https://global.discourse-cdn.com/zscaler/original/2X/2/24ed07b782a70aaaca6d95dd6653b814f3e6aeb7.png)
3. Give your new URL category a name and add “.bing.com” to the Custom URL or URLs retaining parent category and save this URL category. [[33] 33702×901 40.1 KB](https://global.discourse-cdn.com/zscaler/original/2X/f/f00359ff345fdacd0ef542e22fda39285a3ae3b4.png)
4. Lastly, scroll down to the bottom of the new SSL inspection rule and set the action to “Do Not Inspect” > “Bypass Other Policies”. Save this SSL Inspection rule and activate the change on the left. [[44] 44733×507 15.3 KB](https://global.discourse-cdn.com/zscaler/original/2X/3/38243ecee736d4becdb7df5e46936a7276f0b209.png)

Exit out of your Edge browser completely and re-open the browser. Your Bing discover plug-in should now work along with the AI chat feature.
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

---

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009iZzWICA0/configuring-an-ipsec-tunnel-in-routeros-mikrotik-router","lastmod":"2023-06-26T15:38:29.000Z","id":"0D54u00009iZzWICA0"} -->
## Configuring an IPSec Tunnel in RouterOS (Mikrotik Router)

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009iZzWICA0/configuring-an-ipsec-tunnel-in-routeros-mikrotik-router
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-06-23T14:46:15.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-06-26T15:38:29.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 3
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>In this walkthrough, my goal is to route a subnet (192.168.2.0/24) through an IPSec tunnel to Zscaler’s Atlanta II node.</p><p><br></p><h1><strong>Within the ZIA Portal</strong></h1><h2>Define Your Location</h2><ul><li>Navigate to Administration -&gt; VPN Credentials</li></ul><ol><li>Keep FQDN checked<ol><li>Provide a User ID and domain</li><li>Create a Pre-Shared Key (you will need this again later).&nbsp;I used <a href="https://www.gigacalculator.com/randomizers/random-alphanumeric-generator.php" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">this site</a> to create a randomized 30-character alphanumeric key.</li></ol></li></ol><ul><li>Navigate to Administration -&gt; Location Management</li></ul><ol><li>Make sure you associate the newly created VPN Credentials with this location.</li></ol><h1><strong>Within RouterOS</strong></h1><h2>Establish IPSec Tunnel Connectivity</h2><ul><li>Log in to your Mikrotik router console. The default address is 192.168.88.1.&nbsp;You can run the following commands (click Terminal in the top right) to build the required configuration or use the GUI.</li><li><strong>Turn on Safe Mode!&nbsp;</strong>If you make a configuration error that causes you to lose the ability to connect to your router, that change will be reverted automatically while in safe mode.&nbsp;The alternative is having to physically reset your router to factory settings.</li></ul><p><br></p><ul><li>Create the IPSec Profile. You can paste this exactly into the terminal.<ul><li>/ip ipsec profile add dh-group=modp1024 dpd-interval=30s <strong>name</strong>="Zscaler Profile" </li></ul></li><li>Create the Zscaler IPSec Peer.&nbsp;Use <a href="https://config.zscaler.com/zscalertwo.net/cenr" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">this site</a> to find the node you want to peer with.&nbsp;Make sure to copy the VPN Host Name and not the Proxy Host Name!&nbsp;This example uses Zscaler Atlanta II.<ul><li>/ip ipsec peer add address=<a href="http://atl2-vpn.zscalertwo.net" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">atl2-vpn.zscalertwo.net</a> exchange-mode=ike2 name="ZScaler Atlanta II" profile="Zscaler Profile"</li></ul></li><li>Create the IPSec Proposal. You can paste this exactly into the terminal.<ul><li>/ip ipsec proposal add enc-algorithms=aes-256-cbc,aes-192-cbc,aes-128-cbc,null name="Zscaler Proposal"</li></ul></li><li>Create the IPSec Identity.&nbsp;You must replace the highlighted fields with the configured VPN credentials from the ZIA portal.&nbsp;This example uses the peer I created for Zscaler Atlanta II.<ul><li>/ip ipsec identity add my-id=user-fqdn:[YOURUSER@YOURDOMAIN.COM] <strong>peer</strong>="ZScaler Atlanta II" secret=[YOUR_ALPHANUMERIC_PRE-SHARED_SECRET] </li></ul></li><li>Create the IPSec Policy.&nbsp;In this example, I am only routing subnet 192.168.2.0/24 through the IPSec tunnel.<ul><li>/ip ipsec policy add dst-address=0.0.0.0/0 peer="ZScaler Atlanta II" proposal="Zscaler Proposal" src-address=192.168.2.0/24 tunnel=yes</li></ul></li><li>Create a Firewall NAT rule that accepts IPSec packets.&nbsp;In my example, I want subnet 192.168.2.0/24 to be routed through the IPSec tunnel.<ul><li>/ip firewall nat add action=accept <strong>chain</strong>=srcnat ipsec-policy=out,ipsec src-address=192.168.2.0/24</li></ul></li></ul><p><br></p><p>If your IPSec tunnel has successfully connected to Zscaler, you should see the following…</p><p><br></p><p>…within RouterOS (IP -&gt; IPSec)</p><p><img src="/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000b5OGx?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p>…and within the ZIA Portal (Analytics -&gt; Tunnel Insights -&gt; Logs)</p><p><img src="/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000b5OH7?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

## Should you activate Fallback to GW Domain and activate Failover to the 2nd DC in PAC ?

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009jYibQCAS/should-you-activate-fallback-to-gw-domain-and-activate-failover-to-the-2nd-dc-in-pac-

<p>Hello Zscaler Community,</p><p><br></p><p>I have a Question about this Feature "Fallback to Gateway Domain"</p><p>Should you activate this function in general or do you have to set something else somewhere ?</p><p><br></p><ul><li>Fallback to Gateway Domain: Select this checkbox when PAC proxies cannot be reached for Zscaler Tunnel (Z-Tunnel) 1.0, Zscaler Client Connector falls back to the gateway domain.</li></ul><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/servlet/rtaImage?refid=0EM4u000008Pcey"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>The other Question is what should be the correct order</p><p>?</p><p><br></p><p>We use Custom PAC File and there is a directly accessible&nbsp;list. And also some ByPass Lists for Microsoft Services.</p><p>In first section is directly accessible list and after this is the "Default Traffic Forwarding."</p><p><br></p><p>/* Default Traffic Forwarding. Forwarding to Zen on port 80, but you can use port 9400 also */</p><p>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;return "PROXY ${COUNTRY_GATEWAY}:80; PROXY ${COUNTRY_SECONDARY_GATEWAY}:80; DIRECT";</p><p><br></p><p>After this comes ByPass List with Microsoft Services </p><p>And then in the End "Manual Failover to the Secondary DC" </p><p><br></p><p>/* Manual Failover to Secondary Data Center,&nbsp;However, if the primary data center is unavailable for any other reason, such as ISP issues, latency issues, Microsoft issues etc.*/</p><p>return "PROXY ${SECONDARY_GATEWAY_FX}:80; PROXY ${GATEWAY_FX}:80; DIRECT";</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>Is this influenced by this or does it have nothing to do with each other?</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><br></p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009jYrfzCAC/windows-network-location-awareness","lastmod":"2026-05-04T08:00:04.000Z","id":"0D54u00009jYrfzCAC"} -->
## Windows Network Location Awareness

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009jYrfzCAC/windows-network-location-awareness
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-06-27T12:15:28.000Z
- Last activity: 2026-05-04T08:00:04.000Z
- Answers: 4
- Likes: 5
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>Microsoft Windows Network Location Awareness (NLA) functions to detect when on a public/private/domain network. Windows Defender Firewall implements different firewall rules depending on the network location. Generally, a less restrictive policy applies on the Domain, and unless the machine detects the Domain profile all AD functions (GPO/Kerberos/etc) will not function.</p><p><br></p><p>Therefore, it's important that NLA service functions correctly to detect the Domain. Recently I've seen customers change the default action for Public/Private networks to be DENY, which further restricts this functionality.</p><p><br></p><p>Therefore, this article describes what rules to create in Defender firewall to allow NLA to function with Zscaler Private Access. <a href="https://help.zscaler.com/client-connector/zscaler-client-connector-processes-allowlist" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">This</a> article describes the base firewall rules necessary for Zscaler Client Connector to function, and to connect to the Zero Trust Exchange.</p><p>ZCC will connect to the Zero Trust Exchange and ZCC will intercept traffic based on the application segmentation policy. In general, an App Segment will exist for Active Directory consisting of a wildcard (for DNS) and the FQDNs (for the domain controllers).</p><p>When NLA triggers, it causes Windows to perform the Netlogon process. This consists of the DNS lookup (Which will be intercepted by ZCC/ZPA) and returns the IP addresses of the domain controllers. NLA will then attempt to connect to the domain controllers and authenticate - therefore detecting the Domain, and moving to the Domain network profile.</p><p>The key processes here are NLASVC, NetLogon, and LSASS. Therefore creating firewall rules appropriate for this is necessary.</p><p>In MSDefender Firewall create rules for the following</p><ol><li>Program %systemroot%\system32\lsass.exe</li><li>Service - Network Location Awareness</li><li>Service - Netlogon</li></ol><p>These should be permitted access to the IP range 100.64.0.0/16 or 100.64.1.0/24 if you need to be more restrictive (Active Directory DNS would be one of the first processes Windows will query for, so generally it will result in an IP address in the first 255 of the subnet range).</p><p>It may further be possible to restrict this to the appropriate TCP/UDP ports used for AD Discovery of TCP/88, UDP/88, TCP/389, UDP/389, TCP/445.</p><p><br></p><p>Once the rules have been created, create a registry entry</p><p>HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NlaSvc\Parameters</p><p>Add a DWORD parameter :AlwaysExpectDomainController</p><p>Set value to:1</p><p><br></p><p>This triggers NLA to poll for the domain controller more frequetly.</p><p><br></p><p>Once this is done, Windows will poll for the domain controller on network change, or after ZCC starts, which will then be permitted by the Windows firewall. ZCC can then intercept the traffic and pass through ZTE to the domain. The success of this flow will result in the Domain profile becoming active.</p><p><br></p><p>You can run the following in powershell to trigger the network status change -</p><p><br></p><p>Get-NetAdaptor -physical | Restart-NetAdaptor</p><p><br></p><p>You can run the following in powershell to identify the network profile currently applied -</p><p><br></p><p>Get-NetConnectionProfile</p><p><br></p><p>Video is available <a href="https://youtu.be/PxnwpKGBE8E" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">here</a> to explain this functionality. <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/400385/network-location-awareness-not-detecting-domain-ne" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">This</a> help article from Microsoft covers the registry entries which can effect how NLA functions</p><p><br></p><p><iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/PxnwpKGBE8E" title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" allowfullscreen></iframe></p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

## Power Automate Desktop over ZIA

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009raTpdCAE/power-automate-desktop-over-zia
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-08-08T12:49:56.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-08-21T10:03:28.000Z
- Answers: 5
- Likes: 0
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。

<p>Dear Community</p><p><br></p><p>I am trying to authenticate or bypass the connections of '<em>Microsoft Power Automate Desktop</em>' to the internet over ZIA.</p><p>For those that are not aware of the product.</p><p>The software installs a service in Windows named 'Power Automate service' (UIFlowService) that runs with a local account '<em>NT Service\UIFlowService</em>'.</p><p><br></p><p>To trigger Desktop operations from cloud flows the local client needs to connect to the different services at Microsoft.</p><p>These are outlined in this documentation of Microsoft. ## ZIA: SCIM false Redundant Exports

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009x0ARlCAM/zia-scim-false-redundant-exports
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-09-05T15:19:37.000Z

- Answers: 1

- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>Hi Zscaler Community, </p><p><br></p><p>Recently we migrated to Azure AD and using SCIM provisioning. Some users reported that they were getting policy blocks for URLs that are allowed by the company policy. I checked their accounts in ZIA User management and saw that the default AAD group that all employees get for enforcing the default company policy was not assigned. </p><p><br></p><p>Afterwards I checked that particular AAD group to see if the user was a member of it and he indeed was a member. This means that SCIM should have been synced to ZIA User management and the group should have been assignd in ZIA User Management after the sync. As I said before, user was not assigned the group in ZIA User Management. </p><p><br></p><p>Therefore, I provisioned the AAD group on demand for this specific user and AAD skipped the request and returned a "RedundantExport" as reason. So AAD thinks the group is already properly synced to ZIA User Management. This is not the case. </p><p>How to reproduce:</p><ol><li>Remove AAD group from any account in ZIA User Management. </li><li>Provision that specific group for that specific user in AAD. </li><li>Please find Skip Reason below:</li></ol><p><img src="/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000c4cxJ?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p>Workaround: add the user manually to the group in ZIA User Management. </p><p><br></p><p>Has anyone else experienced this or are you able to reproduce? </p><p><br></p><p>Thanks in advance, </p><p>Kevin. </p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009zgqNaCAI/handling-dns-request-type-any-with-zia-cloud-firewall-and-dns-control","lastmod":"2023-09-25T15:52:33.000Z","id":"0D54u00009zgqNaCAI"} -->
## Handling DNS request type "ANY" with ZIA Cloud Firewall and DNS Control

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009zgqNaCAI/handling-dns-request-type-any-with-zia-cloud-firewall-and-dns-control
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-09-22T20:52:20.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-09-25T15:52:33.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 1
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">What is DNS request type "ANY"?</strong></p><p><br></p><p>The DNS request type "ANY" is an auditing, information, or reconnaissance method of asking a DNS server to return all records for the specified domain. For example, if you make an ANY request for <em>example.com</em> it will return all A, MX, SOA, NS, SPF, TXT and other entries the DNS server has specifically for <em>example.com</em>.</p><p><br></p><p>Sometimes a list of records is quite long and exceeds the 512B standard UDP packet size. In cases like these, the DNS server will return as much as what fits into the UDP-based response and indicate that the record is truncated through the TC flag. This usually prompts the client side to re-send an ANY request via TCP so the entire list of records can be returned.</p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Legitimate and malicious uses of ANY requests</strong></p><p><br></p><p>DNS servers responding to recursive queries have a necessarily limited view of all possible DNS resolutions globally. When queried, a DNS server will seek to resolve any given query by asking another DNS server (and so on) or iterating through the hierarchy of authoritative DNS entries starting from one of the core 13 root resolvers to a top level domain authority for ".com" or ".de" and eventually to the authoritative DNS for "example.com". That authoritative DNS will provide the latest official answer for request like A-record queries that tell the requestor that "example.com" can be found at IP address "1.2.3.4" -- and other information like "there is also an address for sending mail to example.com" (an MX record) etc.</p><p><br></p><p>ANY requests are used to find all the possible record types and their values for a domain in a single request so a user doesn't have to request all possible record types sequentially. This is done legitimately to audit existing records and to quickly assemble or share info.</p><p><br></p><p>Unfortunately, the fact that a single request can result in a disproportionately large response and considering that DNS request sources can be forged, together mean that ANY requests are a way to launch reflective DNS attacks. Also, in simply in generating the response, the DNS server consumes more DNS server resources than regular, one-time queries. Finally, ANY is used by attackers to build a picture of the attack surface of any given organization including multi-tenant ones.</p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Recursive cache resolvers and Zscaler Trusted Resolver (ZTR)</strong></p><p><br></p><p>Because of the niche application of ANY requests and their comparative threat, most DNS services have deprecated the support of ANY requests. This is particularly if true the DNS service are cacheing servers for recursive queries. This is less true of authoritative DNS like those provided by domain registrars who must propagate their clients' DNS entries.</p><p><br></p><p>The Zscaler Trusted Resolver (ZTR) responds to recursive requests from users or DNS forwarders. On the backend, it makes iterative queries and uses DNSSEC when authoritative DNS servers it interacts with supports it. ZTR then caches the values it has been asked for the TTL of the entry so it doesn't need to spend time and resources doing further iterative lookups every time it is asked and the record is remains valid.</p><p><br></p><p>ZTR is not an authoritative&nbsp;DNS&nbsp;provider but queries various authoritative DNS servers to resolve the queries it gets asked. Like any DNS public recursive resolver, ZTR will never have the full list of all possible records for a given domain. So when ZTR receives an ANY request, at most it will respond with what is in the cache.&nbsp;So if ZTR does have a response for ANY that is not a SERVFAIL (null) then it will be any resolutions that have been previously provided that haven't exceeded their TTL.</p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Deprecation of DNS ANY requests and End of Support</strong></p><p><br></p><p>DNS ANY requests are decreasingly supported by DNS resolvers on the internet. This is due to of the above noted security threats, the sensibility of supporting the operation on caching DNS servers, and the added processing required to support a capability of questionable value at best.</p><p><br></p><p>Zscaler Trusted Resolver (ZTR) is targeting a complete End of Support for DNS request type "ANY". Some data centers will no longer support ANY requests at all while others may continue until such time that End of Support is complete.</p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Best practices for ANY type requests</strong></p><p><br></p><p>Due to the deprecation and impending End of Support for ANY type requests on the internet, it is therefore imperative to either no longer send ANY type requests generally (recommended) or bypass the few users who may continue to have a legitimate use for ANY requests from resolving at ZTR. This transits the DNS traffic but the requests still get DNS Control policy applied to them.</p><p><br></p><p>A key caveat is that ZTR is a safe and highly available DNS resolver that is accessible in all Zscaler data centers and very few users should be granted a bypass from ZTR resolutions if that rule is in fact enabled in Cloud Firewall policy (in the console: Policy -> Firewall Control, NAT Control Policy tab).</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000c620T?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p>In NAT Control Policy, create a new rule ranked higher than the system-defined "Zscaler Trusted DNS Resolver". The new, higher ranked rule will take precedence over the ZTR rule which directs all DNS requests to the ZTR (and is directed to ZTR regardless of where the user originally wanted to use as a DNS resolver).</p><p><br></p><p>The new NAT rule needs have the Network Service "DNS" selected as a condition (meaning it will apply to any dest TCP/UDP:53 traffic) and all users or groups or other subset/division of users that will be granted an exception to use ANY type requests.</p><p><br></p><p>The action is destination NAT to port 53. Do not enter an IP address in the action unless you want all DNS queries to go to that location. Using only the port number, the rule essentially says "whatever IP address he user originally wanted but it must be sent via dest:53". One of the two values must be present to complete the action in any case.</p><p><br></p><p>Save and activate the rule. </p><p><br></p><p>This will now transit all DNS for the selected subset of users. All other users will get the subsequent rule (redirect to ZTR for example). All DNS Control security inspections continue to still be applied to this DNS traffic.</p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Remote users with Client Connector and tunnel 2</strong></p><p><br></p><p>For any users using Client Connector -- either remote or at a Location -- tunnel 2 needs to be enabled. Tunnel 2 potentially captures all non-web including DNS traffic and sends it via DTLS tunnel to the Zscaler Public Service Edge.</p><p><br></p><p>This also presents another bypass option: when a Client Connector user needs to make DNS ANY requests <strong>and</strong> the permissions allow then temporarily disabling Client Connector, this would mean that the ANY requests does not come to Zscaler. But it also means no traffic comes to Zscaler while the Client Connector is disabled and is a security risk.</p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

---

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000A0dGk2CQE/best-practice-for-cfw-rules-with-network-application-dpi-detections-as-condition","lastmod":"2023-11-30T20:24:39.000Z","id":"0D54u0000A0dGk2CQE"} -->
## Best practice for CFW rules with network application (DPI) detections as condition

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000A0dGk2CQE/best-practice-for-cfw-rules-with-network-application-dpi-detections-as-condition
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-09-28T13:36:06.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-11-30T20:24:39.000Z
- Answers: 2
- Likes: 2
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Network Apps detections in CFW rules</strong></p><p><br></p><p>The use of deep packet inspection (DPI) in firewall rules was once considered revolutionary more than 15 years ago with the creation of a new type of firewall called "next generation firewalls" or NGFWs. DPI independently identifies applications by looking at a variety of behavioral and statistical aspects of communication and blends this with header and other protocol communication values. This is done to get certainty the application generating the flow and for a corporate decision on whether that application should be allowed or not in certain conditions.</p><p><br></p><p>The nature of independently identifying traffic on the wire without assistance of the endpoints in communication means that some packets of the DPI-investigated flow need to pass on the wire before application identification certainty is achieved. Sometimes the app once identified is allowed and sometimes that app is not allowed. In either cases, these packets "leak" until the identification is complete one way or another.</p><p><br></p><p>Zscaler Cloud Firewall calls the DPI application identification condition in firewall rules "network applications" and anytime network applications are invoked as a rule condition, the above process happens. All firewalls behave this way when DPI is used.</p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Best practice in using Network Apps (DPI) in Zscaler Cloud Firewall (CFW) rules</strong></p><p><br></p><p>Network applications usage in CFW should try to follow one or both of the following principles:</p><ol><li>Network applications should always try to be joined with at least one other CFW rule condition. This can be user/group/department or network service (port and protocol), or source/dest IP address etc</li><li>Rules with network applications should be ranked as low as possible and as close as possible to to default last rule (typically a "block all" catch all rule). This allows first packet identification rules to match and execute sooner and the network app rule to take longer while impacted as few subsequent (lower ranked) rules as possible</li></ol><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Example leading to best practice recommendation</strong></p><p><br></p><p>Take the following example of a non-optimal ranked CFW ruleset:</p><ol><li>Allow network app == SSH</li><li>Block network service == Telnet</li><li>Allow network service == HTTP, HTTPS, DNS</li><li>Block all (default rule setting)</li></ol><p>Since the "Allow network app == SSH" is ranked first without additional criteria then CFW will examine every flow to identify SSH. The application identification may take several packets to identify SSH on potentially many, many flows until a determination that the traffic is or is not that network application. The CFW will keep open these flows until 1 of 2 things happen:&nbsp;</p><p><br></p><p>A). DPI terminates and either identifies or does not fully identify or</p><p>B). The inspected flow suddenly stops&nbsp;before DPI terminates</p><p><br></p><p>This ruleset is not optimally constructed since rule 2 and 3 are first packet identifications and could be excluded from DPI examination -- the CFW could have taken an immediate decision on this port/protocol traffic.</p><p><br></p><p>Additionally, rule 1 is too expansive for its high ranking since so much traffic (all traffic in this example) can potentially match. Another condition should be added to narrow the scope of traffic identification and/or the rule should be lowered to allow the immediate condition matching rules to match and take their actions.</p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Example of Optimally ranked CFW ruleset</strong></p><p><br></p><p>Here is the same ruleset as above but optimally ranked:</p><ol><li>Block network service == Telnet</li><li>Allow network service == HTTP, HTTPS, DNS</li><li>Allow network app == SSH</li><li>Block all (default rule setting)</li></ol><p><br></p><p>In the above example, the "Block network service == Telnet" and "Allow network service == HTTP, HTTPS, DNS" rules are ranked higher. Since these do not use network app conditions, these rules always match on the first packet. This means that all matching flows can be immediately assessed without delay and action taken. Only the remaining subset of flows that do not match rule 1 and 2 enter the traffic identification process.</p><p><br></p><p>Here is the same optimally ranked ruleset but now also optimally conditioned:</p><ol><li>Block network service == Telnet</li><li>Allow network service == HTTP, HTTPS, DNS</li><li>Allow network app == SSH AND network service == SSH</li><li>Block all (default rule setting)</li></ol><p><br></p><p>In this example, the network app condition was paired with the logical AND condition by adding the network service condition to the rule. Here, the firewall only applies DPI traffic identification to flows the are TCP on destination port 22 (the definition of this particular network service). The second condition could have been a user, group, department, source IP, destination IP -- really any other condition narrows the scope of the DPI inspection so this sometimes non-first packet identification is exposed on a limited amount of flows.</p><p><br></p><p>This topic is related to a logging condition <a href="https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u00009evnDdCAI/when-allow-due-to-insufficient-app-data-log-entry-value-appears-and-when-it-does-not" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">When "allow due to insufficient app data" log entry value appears and when it does not.</a></p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000A7AC9cCQG/using-zia-cookiebased-user-authentication-with-cloud-connector","lastmod":"2023-12-05T17:39:29.000Z","id":"0D54u0000A7AC9cCQG"} -->
## Using ZIA cookie-based user authentication with Cloud Connector

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000A7AC9cCQG/using-zia-cookiebased-user-authentication-with-cloud-connector
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2023-10-30T19:27:38.000Z
- Last activity: 2023-12-05T17:39:29.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 0
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>Howdy Folks. Here is a guide for forcing user authentication for browser traffic using the ZIA cookie-based authentication mechanism and the Cloud Connector location/sub-location configuration parameters.</p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><strong>Configuration</strong></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p>In the endpoint:</p><ol><li>Install the Zscaler root certificate into the VM / virtual desktop<ol><li>Windows<ol><li>Double-click: Install for System or Current User in the Trusted Root certificates folder</li></ol></li><li>Linux (Fedora, Amazon WorkSpaces):<ol><li>openssl x509 -in ZscalerRootCertificate-2048-SHA256.crt -out zscaler-root.pem -outform PEM</li><li>sudo mv zscaler-root.pem /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/</li><li>sudo update-ca-trust</li></ol></li></ol></li><li>Install the Zscaler root certificate into any browser that uses its own keystore<ol><li>Firefox:&nbsp;<ol><li>Navigate to Settings and then Privacy and Security. Select View Certificates. Choose Authorities, then Import, and finally select the Zscaler certificate. Choose “Trust this certificate to identify websites.”</li><li>Navigate to Settings and then Privacy and Security. Uncheck “Query OCSP responder…” under the Certificates section. NOTE: This reference architecture requires that SSL inspection be enabled for all traffic from this Location. Therefore, all traffic will be subjected to an OCSP check and the check that Firefox does is redundant.&nbsp;</li><li>(Optional) Enable Firefox to use the OS keystore: Navigate to “about:config”, search for and set “security.enterprise_roots.enabled” to True.</li></ol></li></ol></li></ol><p>&nbsp;</p><p>In the Cloud Connector portal:</p><ol><li>Enable Authentication for the Cloud Connector location or a sub-location</li></ol><p>&nbsp;</p><p>In the ZIA portal:</p><ol><li>(Optional) Create two URL filter policies<ol><li>Enable ZIA > Administration > Advanced Settings > Enable Policy For Unauthenticated Traffic</li><li>Rule #1: Allow Auth Bypass URLs<ol><li>Action: Allow</li><li>Users: Authentication Bypass URL</li></ol></li><li>Rule #2: Block Unauthenticated VDI<ol><li>Action: Block</li><li>Departments: Unauthenticated Transactions</li><li>Location: (CC location)</li></ol></li></ol></li><li>Enable SSL inspection for all traffic from the CC location<ol><li>Action: Inspect</li><li>Location: (CC location)</li><li>(Optional) Block Undecryptable Traffic: True</li></ol></li></ol><p>&nbsp;</p><p><strong>Verification</strong></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p>On a virtual desktop that connects to the Internet via the configured CC location, open a web browser and navigate to any URL. We expect the browser captive portal to be shown and request the user to login to ZIA. Once this is done, checking the site connection details will show a cookie for the customer’s Zscaler cloud.</p><p>&nbsp;</p><p><strong>Important Notes</strong></p><p>&nbsp;</p><p>Note, if the SSL inspection rule is not configured then the browser captive portal will not be shown when navigating via HTTPS. Navigating to an HTTP site such as http://www.neverssl.com will initiate the captive portal. With that said, without the SSL inspection rule, even if the user logs into the captive portal via an HTTP site, subsequent HTTPS page loads will fail because the browser will not include the ZIA cookies in the request (and ZIA cannot inspect the traffic).</p><p><br></p><p><strong>Helpful Links</strong></p><p><br></p><p>https://help.zscaler.com/zia/about-zscaler-cookies</p><p>https://help.zscaler.com/zia/about-provisioning-authenticating-users</p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

## ZIA Bypass/Network Troubleshooting

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AKiBuOCQV/zia-bypassnetwork-troubleshooting
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2024-02-22T15:07:16.000Z
- Last activity: 2024-02-22T19:58:49.000Z
- Answers: 2
- Likes: 0
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>Hi,</p><p> </p><p>We have been working with Zscaler support but feel like we haven't been able to make our situation better; instead, it feels like we are chasing squirrels.</p><p><br></p><p>We are using Tunnel 2.0 with an app profile PAC file and Forwarding PAC file. The PAC files are the same, with the exception of using 'return "Direct"' in the app PAC and 'return "Proxy ${ZAPP_TUNNEL2_BYPASS}"' in the forwarding PAC for traffic intended to bypass Zscaler.</p><p><br></p><p>We have also tried removing some of the URLs we want to bypass Zscaler from the app PAC and adding it to the 'Hostname or IP Address Bypass for VPN Gateway." But those sites are still showing up in the web insight logs as going through Zscaler. </p><p><br></p><p>In the forwarding profile, we have the 'System Proxy Settings' configured with 'Enforce' and have the forwarding PAC applied as the 'Use Automatic Configuration Script.'</p><p><br></p><p>Most of these configurations were suggested by Zscaler support, but as I am reading more and more articles. It seems that ZTunnel 2.0 conflicts with having a Forward PAC and the 'Enforce - System Proxy" action. </p><p> </p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g4fAL?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p>Obviously, I am missing something; if anyone has suggestions or notes, I would love to test them in our environment. We are entirely remote, so each user is on their own ISP, and we are hoping to figure out how to correctly bypass Zscaler for some domains to alleviate some networking pains. </p><p><br></p><p>Thanks!</p>

## How To: Tunnel-less DNS Resolution using DNS Control/ZTR (Guest WiFi Users)

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AM6064CQB/how-to-tunnelless-dns-resolution-using-dns-controlztr-guest-wifi-users
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2024-03-07T22:32:19.000Z
- Last activity: 2025-10-01T18:06:51.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 2
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>In this article, we will see how one can achieve tunnel-less DNS resolution by sending DNS queries to Zscaler DNS Control/ZTR without having to create a GRE tunnel.</p><p><br></p><p>This tunnel-less approach can be beneficial when migrating from <a href="https://help.zscaler.com/eos-eol/eos-eol-notice-zscaler-shift" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Zscaler Shift (now EOL)</a> or a 3rd party resolver, or when using a GRE/IPsec tunnel from a customer site is not an option. However, it is important to note that the recommended practice is to use Zscaler Client Connector with Z-Tunnel 2.0 (ZCC/ZT2.0) or a GRE/IPsec tunnel to route DNS traffic to ZIA whenever possible.</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gLb?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note: </strong>This tunnel-less DNS solution is not applicable for DNS over HTTPS (DoH) traffic.</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><h2><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Steps to Configure DNS Control/ZTR&nbsp;</strong></h2><p><br></p><p><strong>Configure DNS server addresses on client machine</strong></p><p>First, find out the GRE VIP addresses for the Zscaler data center closest to your network.</p><p>For this,&nbsp;go to&nbsp;<a href="https://config.zscaler.com/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://config.zscaler.com/</a>&nbsp;and select your ZIA cloud.&nbsp;In my setup, it is zscalertwo.net:</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gMG?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>Now, go down to the data center closest your network and note down the GRE VIP addresses. Here I have chosen the San Francisco IV data center:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gMK?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note: </strong>You can also automate&nbsp;this using JSON API:</p><p><a href="https://help.zscaler.com/zia/zscaler-service-endpoints" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://help.zscaler.com/zia/zscaler-service-endpoints</a></p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note: </strong>This tunnel-less DNS solution is not applicable for IPv6 DNS traffic.</p><p><br></p><p>On your client machine (or internal DNS forwarder), configure these GRE VIP addresses as the DNS server addresses:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gMU?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p>Here we have configured the DNS server addresses on a Windows client machine.</p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note:</strong> In this deployment scenario, the client machine is NOT using ZCC.&nbsp;If the client is using ZCC with Z-Tunnel 2.0, then you should really not have a need to do it this way.&nbsp;</p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note:</strong> Here we chose the GRE VIP addresses from the same data center, however, you can also choose the GRE VIP addresses from two different data centers for resiliency.</p><p><br></p><p><strong>Configure your ZIA Tenant</strong></p><p>In our ZIA tenant, we need to define the location for the public IP of our client.</p><p><br></p><p>First, navigate to&nbsp;Administration > Resources > Static IPs &amp; GRE Tunnels. Then, click on Add Static IP:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gO1?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p>Specify the public IP of your location as will be seen by the ZIA tenant, give a name and click Next:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gOB?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>Specify the region and click Next.</p><p>Review and save.</p><p><br></p><p>Now, navigate to Administration > Resources > Location Management:</p><p>Under Locations tab: Click on Add Location:&nbsp;</p><p>Create a new location as shown and under "Static IP Addresses and GRE Tunnels",&nbsp;choose the Static IP that you had created earlier:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gPA?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note: Additionally, enable "Enforce Firewall Control" option:</strong></p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gPZ?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong>Firewall, DNS and NAT Policies</strong></p><p>Additionally, here are the screenshots for Firewall, DNS and NAT rules for reference.&nbsp;</p><p>Make sure that DNS traffic is allowed as shown by the below rules.</p><p><br></p><p><strong><em>Firewall Filtering:</em></strong></p><p><br></p><p>Note rule no 3 that allows DNS, HTTP and HTTPS traffic:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gQ8?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><strong><em>DNS Control:</em></strong></p><p>By default, you have the following rules in your ZIA tenant to allow DNS traffic.&nbsp;</p><p>Do not add any DNS filtering rules at this stage, instead, first verify that DNS resolution is working as expected, and then you can add DNS filtering rules later on.</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gQX?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px; font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &quot;Segoe UI&quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, &quot;Fira Sans&quot;, &quot;Droid Sans&quot;, &quot;Helvetica Neue&quot;, sans-serif;"><em>NAT Control:&nbsp;</em></strong></p><p><br></p><p><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gSJ?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note:&nbsp;</strong>Make sure default DNAT rule is present and enabled as shown above. This DNAT rule is what sends the DNS traffic to ZTR.</p><p>See the following for reference:</p><p><a href="https://help.zscaler.com/zia/about-nat-control" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://help.zscaler.com/zia/about-nat-control</a></p><p><br></p><h2><strong>Verification of basic DNS resolution:</strong></h2><p>On the client machine, initiate DNS lookups:</p><p><br></p><p><strong><img src="/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gU0?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></strong></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>In a following article, we will see how you can add a DNS Control policy to block access to certain restricted sites, such as gambling:</p><p><br></p><p><a href="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/s/question/0D54u0000AM61y5CQB/how-to-configure-dns-control-policies-for-tunnelless-dns-setup-guest-wifi-users" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/s/question/0D54u0000AM61y5CQB/how-to-configure-dns-control-policies-for-tunnelless-dns-setup-guest-wifi-users</a></p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

<!-- ZS-POST {"url":"https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AM61y5CQB/how-to-configure-dns-control-policies-for-tunnelless-dns-setup-guest-wifi-users","lastmod":"2026-03-17T19:16:31.000Z","id":"0D54u0000AM61y5CQB"} -->
## How To: Configure DNS Control policies for tunnel-less DNS setup (Guest WiFi users)

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AM61y5CQB/how-to-configure-dns-control-policies-for-tunnelless-dns-setup-guest-wifi-users
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2024-03-08T00:15:40.000Z
- Last activity: 2026-03-17T19:16:31.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 4
- Status: closed
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>In an earlier article, we configured DNS resolution using Zscaler Trusted Resolver (ZTR) using a tunnel-less DNS setup:</p><p><br></p><p><a href="https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AM6064CQB/how-to-tunnelless-dns-resolution-using-dns-controlztr-guest-wifi-users" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AM6064CQB/how-to-tunnelless-dns-resolution-using-dns-controlztr-guest-wifi-users</a></p><p><br></p><p>This tunnel-less approach can be beneficial when migrating from <a href="https://help.zscaler.com/eos-eol/eos-eol-notice-zscaler-shift" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">Zscaler Shift (now EOL)</a> or a 3rd party resolver, or when using a GRE/IPsec tunnel from a customer site is not an option. However, it is important to note that the recommended practice is to use Zscaler Client Connector with Z-Tunnel 2.0 (ZCC/ZT2.0) or a GRE/IPsec tunnel to route DNS traffic to ZIA whenever possible.</p><p><br></p><p>This article builds upon the configuration in the previous article, so make sure to complete those steps before proceeding further.</p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note: </strong>This tunnel-less DNS approach has the following limitations:</p><ul><li>It is not applicable for DNS over HTTPS (DoH) traffic.</li><li>It is not applicable for IPv6 DNS traffic.</li></ul><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/Zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gjP?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>In this article, we will build upon that setup and add a DNS filtering rule to block gambling sites.</p><p><br></p><p>First, confirm that DNS resolution for a gambling site, such as 888.com is currently working on your client machine.</p><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/Zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gjy?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p>As one can see, DNS resolution is working and the DNS server is the one we had configured.</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong>Configure DNS Control policy</strong></p><p><br></p><p>Now, in your ZIA tenant, go to <strong>Policy > Firewall > DNS Control</strong>.</p><p><br></p><p>Then, click on <strong>Add DNS Filtering Rule</strong> and add a new rule as shown below:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/068PJ00000Sb53r?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>Make sure to set the rule order number to be higher than the default one that allows all DNS traffic.</p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note:</strong> Zscaler supports different types of End User Notifications (EUNs) for the DNS Control policy. These EUNs are displayed to end users when their activities trigger DNS Control rules with specific actions, such as blocking traffic or redirecting responses.&nbsp;See the following help articles:</p><p><a href="https://help.zscaler.com/zia/dns-end-user-notifications" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://help.zscaler.com/zia/dns-end-user-notifications</a></p><p><a href="https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-dns-control-policy" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-dns-control-policy</a></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>Save the rule and click on <strong>Activation > Activate</strong> to activate the changes.</p><p><br></p><p>Now, go back to the client machine and try doing a DNS lookup for 888.com - it should be blocked:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/068PJ00000Sb58g?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Recommended next steps</strong></p><p><br></p><p>You can implement DNS filtering based on the recommended best practices:</p><p><a href="https://help.zscaler.com/zia/best-practices-dns-control-rules" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://help.zscaler.com/zia/best-practices-dns-control-rules</a></p><p><br></p><p>Additionally, DNS control policies for some of these best practices should now be available by default in your ZIA tenant:</p><ul><li>Critical risk DNS categories</li><li>Critical risk DNS tunnels</li><li>High risk DNS categories</li><li>High risk DNS tunnels</li><li>Risky DNS categories</li><li>Risky DNS tunnels</li></ul><p>You can choose to either enable all or select the ones that meet your deployment needs.</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Additional References</strong></p><p><br></p><p>Zscaler DNS Security and Control Reference Architecture Guide:</p><p><a href="https://www.zscaler.com/resources/reference-architectures/zscaler-dns-security-and-control-reference-architecture.pdf" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank" style="font-size: small; font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;">https://www.zscaler.com/resources/reference-architectures/zscaler-dns-security-and-control-reference-architecture.pdf</a></p>
<!-- /ZS-POST -->

## How To: Differentiated DNS Control Policy for Guest Wi-Fi Users (Tunnel-less DNS Setup)

- Source: https://community.zscaler.com/s/question/0D54u0000AM63EtCQJ/how-to-differentiated-dns-control-policy-for-guest-wifi-users-tunnelless-dns-setup
- Type: Q&A
- Posted: 2024-03-08T01:28:17.000Z
- Last activity: 2024-03-08T01:28:17.000Z
- Answers: 0
- Likes: 0
- Note: ユーザー投稿であり Zscaler の公式見解ではない。内容が古い場合があるため投稿日を確認すること。
- Note: 回答本文は UI API では取得できないため未収録。

<p>In earlier articles, we saw how you can&nbsp;achieve tunnel-less DNS resolution by sending DNS queries to Zscaler DNS Control/ZTR without having to create a GRE tunnel, and apply DNS Control policies to such DNS traffic:</p><p><br></p><p><a href="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/s/question/0D54u0000AM6064CQB/how-to-tunnelless-dns-resolution-using-dns-controlztr-guest-wifi-users" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/s/question/0D54u0000AM6064CQB/how-to-tunnelless-dns-resolution-using-dns-controlztr-guest-wifi-users</a></p><p><br></p><p><a href="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/s/question/0D54u0000AM61y5CQB/how-to-configure-dns-control-policies-for-tunnelless-dns-setup-guest-wifi-users" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank">https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/s/question/0D54u0000AM61y5CQB/how-to-configure-dns-control-policies-for-tunnelless-dns-setup-guest-wifi-users</a></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gri?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>This is especially useful, when migrating from a DNS provider, such as Zscaler Shift (now approaching EOL) or a 3rd party DNS resolver, to Zscaler DNS Control/ZTR.</p><p><br></p><p>One of the common requirements of such a "tunnel-less" DNS deployment is to have differentiated DNS Control policies based on the type of user or devices, such as different polices for guests/contractors vs. authorized users vs. IOT devices.</p><p><br></p><p><strong>The challenge is that since all these users would reach the ZIA cloud using a common public IP, how can we distinguish them in ZIA tenant?&nbsp;</strong></p><p><br></p><p>This can be achieved by assigning different GRE VIP addresses as DNS server addresses to the various clients/devices, and then by matching based on this GRE VIP address (in addition to the location) while selecting the DNS Control policy to be applied.</p><p><br></p><p>Let us look at a scenario of applying two different DNS Control policies to two different set of users:</p><p><br></p><ul><li>Guest users: Block access to gambling sites</li><li>Authorized users: Allow access to gambling sites</li></ul><p><br></p><p>This is just a simple example, the actual polices can vary depending on the requirements.</p><p><br></p><p><strong>Note:</strong>&nbsp;Here we are assuming you have a working tunnel-less DNS setup and have already configured a location for the public IP of the users and enabled firewall control for that location in the ZIA Cloud.</p><p>See the above articles for details.</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong style="font-size: 14px;">Configure DNS server addresses</strong></p><p><br></p><p><strong>DNS server addresses for guest users</strong></p><p>For example, we can assign the following two GRE VIP addresses (from two different data centers for high-availability) to the guest users:</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gsH?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gVE?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p>On the client machine, configure these GRE VIP addresses as the DNS server addresses:</p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gsq?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><strong>DNS server addresses for authorized users</strong></p><p>Similarly,&nbsp;we can assign the following GRE VIP address to authorized users:</p><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gt0?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p><br></p><p><img src="https://community.zscaler.com/zenith/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/0684u00000g5gtA?asPdf=false&amp;operationContext=CHATTER"></p><p><br></p><p>On the client machine, configure these GRE VIP addresses as the DNS server addresses:</p><p><br></p><p><img
